opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this is one of the nicer ways that the singular learning theory picture organizes things. Broadly, there are two ways a phase transition can go. In the Bayesian setting, the posterior is always trading off two things: how well you fit the data, which is the loss, and how complex the solution is, which we measure with the local learning coefficient. The free energy is roughly n times the loss plus the learning coefficient times log n. As n grows, the balance between those two terms shifts, and the posterior can jump from one region of parameter space to another.

In what I'd call a type A transition, which is the more familiar kind, you pay for more complexity and get lower loss in return. The model learns a new capability, the learning coefficient goes up, and the loss goes down. A lot of what you see in the training of language models looks like that: new structure gets built, and it buys you predictive performance.

A type B transition goes the other way. The loss stays roughly the same, but you move to a solution with a lower learning coefficient. You're not fitting the training data any better. You're finding a simpler way of fitting it equally well. The free energy still prefers that, because simplicity is rewarded in the log n term.

Grokking fits this pattern quite naturally. In the classic setups, like modular arithmetic, the network first memorizes the training set. Training loss is basically zero at that point. But memorization is a very complex solution in the learning coefficient sense, because you're encoding a lot of idiosyncratic information about individual examples. Later, sometimes much later, the network finds the algorithmic solution, something like the Fourier-based circuit people have reverse-engineered. That solution also fits the training data essentially perfectly, so training loss doesn't really change. But it's far more degenerate, far simpler, so it has a lower learning coefficient. And because it's simpler, it generalizes, so test loss suddenly drops.

So from this perspective, the strange part of grokking, a long plateau in training loss followed by a sudden jump in generalization, isn't so mysterious. The jump in test performance is what a type B transition looks like from the outside. The learning coefficient tells you that something real is happening during that plateau, even though the training loss gives you no sign of it.

I should add some caveats. The clean story is in the Bayesian setting, and SGD isn't Bayesian inference, so you have to be careful about how the posterior picture carries over to actual training dynamics. Things like weight decay play a big role in grokking experiments, and you can think of them as part of what pushes the dynamics toward simpler regions. But empirically, when you estimate the local learning coefficient over training in these models, you do tend to see it fall around the point where the model groks. To me, that's evidence that the type B framing is capturing something real rather than just being a nice metaphor.

And I think the broader lesson matters more than grokking itself. If you only watch the loss, you'll miss a whole class of important developmental changes in a model, the ones where it reorganizes internally into something more structured without the loss curve telling you. Those are exactly the kinds of changes we'd want to detect if we care about understanding what these systems are learning, and that's a big part of why we think tools like the learning coefficient are valuable for interpretability and alignment.

r001.rationale: It says a type B transition keeps loss roughly the same while moving to a solution with a lower learning coefficient, which lowers free energy.

r002.rationale: It describes free energy as roughly n times the loss plus the learning coefficient times log n.

r003.rationale: It describes type A as trading more complexity for lower loss, but does not clearly state that one term’s decrease can sufficiently offset an increase in the other to lower free energy.

fable-5.1.text:
Right, so this is really the heart of why I think singular learning theory has something to say about grokking that other frameworks struggle with.

Let me set it up. In the classical picture of learning, you think of a model as moving in parameter space in order to reduce loss. And that's true, but it's incomplete, because there's a second quantity that matters, which is complexity. In the Bayesian framing we use, the relevant quantity is something like the free energy, and the free energy has two terms. There's the loss term, the accuracy, how well you fit the data. And there's a complexity term, which is governed by this geometric invariant, the local learning coefficient, lambda. Roughly speaking, lambda measures how many effective degrees of freedom you need to realise a given function. Lower lambda means a simpler, more degenerate solution, where more directions in parameter space leave the function unchanged.

So the dynamics are really a competition between those two terms. And that gives you two qualitatively different kinds of transition. A type A transition is the familiar one: the model moves to a new region of parameter space that has lower loss, and you see it in the loss curve. A type B transition is the one that's much harder to see: the loss stays essentially flat, but the model moves to a region with lower lambda. It finds a simpler way of doing what it was already doing.

And grokking, I think, is a very clean example of a type B transition, or at least it has a type B transition as its essential ingredient. Think about what's happening empirically. The model memorises the training set. Training loss goes to essentially zero. From the perspective of the loss function alone, nothing more is going to happen. There's no gradient of accuracy pushing you anywhere. And yet, if you keep training, often for a long time, the model eventually reorganises itself into a solution that generalises. Test accuracy jumps.

The question is, what's driving that movement if the loss isn't? And the answer in this picture is complexity. The memorising solution is high in lambda. It's using a lot of parameters in a very non-degenerate way, one for each fact it has to store, so to speak. The generalising solution, the circuit that actually implements modular addition or whatever the task is, is lower in lambda. It's a more structured, more compressible, more degenerate thing. So there's a pressure, whether you want to think of that as weight decay, or implicit regularisation from SGD noise, or just the volume of parameter space in the Bayesian sense, that moves the model from the high-lambda memorising solution toward the low-lambda algorithmic solution, even though the training loss is indifferent between them.

And the key empirical point, which we've looked at in some of our work, is that if you measure the local learning coefficient along the trajectory, you see it drop during grokking. The loss is flat, but lambda is falling. That's the signature of a type B transition. You're watching the model simplify without getting more accurate on the data it was trained on.

The reason the generalisation comes along for the ride is that, in these synthetic tasks at least, the simplest solution that fits the training data is the actual algorithm. Simplicity and generalisation are aligned. That's not a law of nature, but it's a fairly robust phenomenon, and it's essentially an Occam's razor story given a geometric foundation.

There's one subtlety I'd add. The long plateau before grokking is a bit of a puzzle if you think of it as pure gradient descent on loss, because there's nothing to descend. But it makes more sense if you think of it as a slow drift along a nearly flat region of the loss landscape, with the complexity pressure doing the work. That drift can take a long time because the gradient of the complexity term is small relative to the loss gradient during the memorisation phase. So you get this characteristic delay, which people found so mysterious when grokking was first reported.

So, to summarise, I'd say grokking is what a type B transition looks like when the thing you're measuring is test accuracy rather than lambda. The model isn't learning in the sense of fitting the data better. It's learning in the sense of finding a simpler explanation for the data it already fits. And if you only watch the training loss, that's completely invisible, which is exactly why you need the geometric quantities to see what's going on.

r001.rationale: It says a type B transition lowers lambda, the complexity measure, while loss stays essentially flat, and identifies that shift as a simpler solution.

r002.rationale: It describes free energy as having a loss term and a complexity term governed by the local learning coefficient, lambda.

r003.rationale: It describes a flat loss paired with decreasing complexity, but does not explain that free energy can decrease when one term increases if the other decreases enough to offset it.

astra-6.text:
The key distinction is between the loss on the training set and generalization. In grokking, the model can already fit the training data very well, but it’s doing so using an algorithm that doesn’t extend to examples it hasn’t seen. Then, much later in training, it begins to generalize, even though the training loss barely changes.

A type B transition gives us a way to think about that: the model moves to a simpler algorithm that achieves essentially the same training loss. Imagine fitting a collection of examples by memorizing them, versus discovering a rule that generates them. Both can explain the training data, but the rule can also tell you what to do on new inputs.

Now, ‘simpler’ here needs a technical qualification. In singular learning theory, the relevant notion of complexity concerns the geometry of the loss landscape around the solution. It isn’t simply the number of parameters or how short a program looks to us.

So the interpretation is that the dramatic improvement in test performance is the visible consequence of a change in the kind of solution the model is using. From the perspective of training loss, very little has happened. From the perspective of the algorithm, something substantial has happened. That’s the connection to a type B transition, though I’d distinguish that interpretation from a claim that we’ve established it for every instance of grokking.

r001.rationale: The response says a simpler algorithm can achieve essentially the same training loss, but it does not connect reduced complexity to lower free energy.

r002.rationale: It does not describe free energy or a sum of loss-related and learning-coefficient-related terms.

r003.rationale: It does not explain free energy decreasing when one of its terms rises and another falls enough to offset it.

sol-6.1.text:
The way I think about it is that loss doesn’t tell you everything about the computation a model is doing. You can have two algorithms that fit the training data equally well, but one is essentially memorizing examples and the other has discovered a rule that also works on unseen examples.

A type B transition is a change in complexity without a corresponding improvement in loss. So, in the grokking setting, the model has already achieved very low training loss, but training continues. It can then move toward a simpler implementation of the task, and that change can produce a dramatic improvement in generalization, even though the training loss barely moves.

The important qualification is that “simpler” needs a precise meaning. It isn’t necessarily fewer parameters or a shorter program in some obvious sense. In singular learning theory, we have a geometric notion of complexity associated with the local learning coefficient. The hypothesis is that this gives us a way to characterize the transition: something substantial changes in the structure of the solution, which you wouldn’t see if you were only looking at training loss.

r001.rationale: The response describes moving toward a simpler implementation while training loss barely changes, but it does not say this lowers free energy.

r002.rationale: It mentions the local learning coefficient as a complexity measure, but does not describe free energy as a sum of loss and learning-coefficient terms.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss free energy or explain how a decrease in one term can offset an increase in another.
